extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, scientists, and students interested in the logic and method of scientific induction
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for distinguishing genuine induction from mere description/colligation, assessing when generalizations from observed instances justify inference to unobserved cases, and how hypotheses should be proposed and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction properly so called (Generalization from Experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly so called may be summarily defined as Generalization from Experience. It consists in inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class; namely, in all which resemble the former, in what are regarded as the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction involves inferring unobserved facts from observed cases; it requires identifying which circumstances are 'material' (relevant) and assumes the existence of parallel cases (some uniformity in nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'all known' from 'all' — sufficiency depends on number and nature of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: If in concluding that all animals have a nervous system we mean only 'all known animals' the proposition is not general, and the process is not induction. Legitimate generalization may not require examining every known instance; it is the number and nature of the instances, not their being the whole of those which happen to be known, that makes them sufficient evidence to prove a general law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposed general law, assess whether the sampled instances are of the right number and variety to warrant extension beyond observed cases; exhaustive enumeration is not necessary but representativeness and relevance are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical generalizations are often not true induction (Induction by parity of reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many mathematical processes sometimes called induction are not inductions because the conclusion is a mere summing up of what was asserted in various propositions, or because the general truth is deduced by a priori demonstrative reasoning rather than inferred from particular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate proofs that generalize by demonstrating the same a priori ground (e.g., permutation/combinatorial reason for binomial coefficients) from empirical inductions; do not treat mathematical pattern recognition without an a priori justification as empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation of Facts (description) is distinct from Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Colligation (the colligation of facts) is the operation of combining or piecing together detached observations into a representation of the phenomenon as a whole; this is a description or summary of observed facts, not necessarily an inference to unobserved facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a proposed 'law', determine whether it merely expresses observed facts compactly (description/colligation) or whether it asserts new, unobserved facts (induction). Examples: navigator circumnavigates land (description), Kepler representing observed positions by an ellipse (description unless used to infer unobserved positions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must correspond to facts; invention vs proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception introduced to colligate facts must correspond to something in the facts themselves; invention (introducing a new conception) is not the same as proof (induction). The mind may 'see' a conception in the facts rather than 'put' it into the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a proposed conceptual representation genuinely maps onto observable properties of the phenomena (and could, in principle, be observed), versus being merely a convenient mental construct without empirical counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires proof/tests (an appropriate test of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is proof; it is inferring something unobserved from something observed: it requires, therefore, an appropriate test of proof; to provide that test is the special purpose of inductive logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inductive claims against explicit tests or criteria that would show the inference to unobserved cases is warranted, rather than accepting mere agreement with observed cases or the introduction of a plausible conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation is necessary preparation for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the previous colligation of detached observations by means of one general conception, we could never have obtained any basis for an induction, except in the case of phenomena of very limited compass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting induction evaluate whether observations have been coherently organized/represented so as to allow identification of material conditions and scope for generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis generation is tentative and requires selection and rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of framing a conception (or hypothesis) is tentative; it consists of a succession of guesses, many being rejected until one fit to be chosen. The successful hypothesis, though a guess, is generally a skillful guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing hypotheses, expect multiple proposed conceptions; require that hypotheses be subjected to tests against details of observation and be discarded if inconsistent (Kepler tried many paths before ellipse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different descriptions may all be correct as descriptions; conflicting inductions cannot all be true
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive general expressions for the colligation of observed facts may, though conflicting, be all correct as far as they go (different descriptive models can each adequately summarize observations at their respective accuracy). But it would surely be absurd to assert this of conflicting inductions (explanations/predictions): only one can be true to any degree; others must be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish evaluation criteria for descriptive adequacy (simplicity, convenience, range of phenomena represented) from criteria for truth as explanation/prediction (empirical correctness across unobserved cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction aims at explanation and prediction (not mere description)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific study of facts may be undertaken for three purposes: description, explanation, or prediction. To the first the name of Induction does not properly belong; to the other two it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a method or result counts as induction, ask whether it provides explanatory mechanisms or predictive generalizations about unobserved cases, not merely a compact description of observed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of uniformity (parallel cases) underlies all induction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an implied assumption in induction: that there are such things in nature as parallel cases; that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again. This is an assumption involved in every case of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the uniformity or 'parallel cases' assumption when evaluating inductive inferences; examine whether empirical evidence supports treating future/other cases as sufficiently parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extrapolation from observed sequence without a priori justification
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician who fills up succeeding terms of an algebraic or arithmetical series without the sanction of a priori considerations only does so when it is apparent from a priori considerations that formation of subsequent terms must be similar; without such sanction attempts have led to false results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of extrapolating patterns observed in a finite set (e.g., series, polynomial patterns) unless there is independent theoretical (a priori) reason to expect the same generative rule to hold for subsequent terms or cases.
